summary: CITS1401 is UWA's first-year Python unit (Python 3, Thonny IDE, Moodle auto-graded labs and projects, closed-book pen-and-paper final worth 50-60%). Lecture order follows John Zelle's "Python Programming: An Introduction to Computer Science" (3e) slide deck, reordered by the coordinators: intro/software process -> variables, expressions, types -> definite for loops (range) -> math module -> if/elif/else and boolean logic -> functions (def/return/parameters, docstrings) -> strings and string methods -> lists/tuples/sequences -> text file processing -> functions part 2 (scope, multiple returns) -> indefinite while loops, nested loops -> exceptions (try/except) -> lists and dictionaries -> simulation/design -> objects/graphics -> search algorithms -> recursion. Five Moodle lab quizzes (MCQ, select-all, predict-output, fill-in-blank, CodeRunner write-a-function with test tables) mirror that order: Lab 01 Python basics, Lab 02 Functions, Lab 03 Conditions and simple loops, Lab 04 strings/lists/tuples, Lab 05 dictionaries and files. Two CSV data-processing projects (15% + 20%) are auto-tested on Moodle by calling a mandatory top-level main(csvfile, ...) that must return lists/tuples/dicts; rules verified verbatim across 2020, 2022, 2023 specs: no imports of any module (even csv/math), never call input(), never call print() except on graceful termination, round only at output to 4 dp, don't assume a .csv extension, locate columns by header name, case-insensitive strings, skip invalid rows, terminate gracefully returning empty/None. So students hand-write CSV splitting, mean/std/standard error, cosine similarity, ranking with tie-breaks, and sorting. Marking: 22/30 automated tests + 5 style + 3 efficiency, with -4 if the marker has to fix a crash. Exams are 8 write-a-function questions (5-20 marks each) with no imports, escalating from string manipulation, palindromes, dict-to-sorted-list-of-tuples, mandatory recursion, series-with-tolerance while loops, nested-list recursion, triple nested loop combinations, to a file read/write question with try/except and header-index lookup. Older exams (2017) also had predict-the-output and explain/rewrite-this-code questions. A separate "no global variables" rule was NOT found in any spec; treat it as a style expectation only.

findings.detail: CITS1401 Computational Thinking with Python, Level 1 core for CS/Data Science/Engineering etc. Coordinators: Dr Ghulam Mubashar Hassan (S1), Dr Jake Kendrick (S2). Contact: 2h lectures + 2h lab + 1h workshop per week. Outcomes: create algorithms using computational thinking; write Python 3 programs; demonstrate computational problem solving. Handbook lists indicative assessment as projects, labs, final examination, and a competency test (must score >=50% overall AND meet the competency test requirement to pass). The CITX1401 (online) variant lists mid-semester test, projects and laboratories, final examination.

findings.topic: Lab sequence and content (assessed Moodle quizzes)
findings.detail: Lab 00 Introduction (Moodle setup). Lab 01 'Python basics': operator precedence, int/float/str types, int('12.0') error, valid identifiers, assignment statements, trace variable values. Lab 02 'Functions in Python': def/docstring/return/parameters vs arguments, local variables, built-ins abs/round/int, fill-in-blank on function definitions. Lab 03 'Conditions and simple loops': comparison/boolean operators, `in`, string comparison, elif semantics True/False, select-all-syntactically-incorrect blocks, predict output, equivalent nested-if blocks, CodeRunner tasks my_abs(value), is_odd(number), bmi_risk(bmi, age), buy_goods(cost, savings), rewrite nested ifs as single if-else. Lab 04 (2022 solutions): strings/lists/tuples, e.g. find_word(sentence, word) using .find, sorted_items(data), cubed_tuple(number) returning a tuple. Lab 05 (2022 solutions): dictionaries and files, e.g. get_name(dic, key) with .get, make_dictionary(filename) word-count from a text file, run_length_encode(nums) returning list of (item,count) tuples, singleDigit(N) digit-sum loop, plus books.csv and an 'objects' lab zip. 2020 lab files show the same arc: lab1 loops (sum of Fibonacci/squares), lab2 functions (tripCost, oddfinder), lab3 while/maths (gcd, binary conversion, composites), lab4 lists (insertion sort with tie-break by name, intersect, swap), lab5 dictionaries (max/min over dict of lists).
findings.source: Newguinea/cits1401 lab/ PDFs and Q*.py files; brayden-blackham/Cits1401 lab1-lab5

findings.topic: Lab question formats (for the app to imitate)
findings.detail: Moodle quiz pages mix: (a) single-answer MCQ ('Which data type will be output of a = 4 // 2'); (b) select-ALL-that-apply (which code blocks are syntactically incorrect / equivalent); (c) True/False on semantics; (d) numeric/short-answer 'What is printed after executing the code below? Try to answer without trying it out'; (e) fill-in-the-blank on code vocabulary (function name, parameters); (f) CodeRunner 'Write a function X(...)' with a Test/Result table (e.g. print(is_odd(-321)) -> True) and a 'penalty regime: 0, 10, ... %' per failed check. Each question is worth 1 mark and can be re-checked.
findings.source: Newguinea/cits1401 lab/lab1 and lab/lab3 PDFs (Moodle exports, CITS1401 2022S2)

findings.topic: Project rule set (verified verbatim, consistent 2020-2023, echoed in 2024/2026 snippets)
findings.detail: 1) 'Your program must define the function main with the following signature/syntax: def main(csvfile...)'; 'if you fail to define main(), the testing program will not be able to test your code and your submission will be graded zero'. 2) 'You are not allowed to import any Python module' (2023: 'any external or internal module in python'), justified as 'getting practice opening text files, processing text file data, and use of basic Python structures, in this case lists and loops'. 3) 'Ensure your program does NOT call the input() function at any time' (marker detects it and won't test). 4) 'Your program should also not call the print() function at any time' except (2022 P2/2023) 'for the case of graceful termination'; never print outputs instead of returning them. 5) 'All returned lists must contain numerical values rounded to four decimal places... not to round the values during calculations and round them only at the time of saving them in the output lists'. 6) 'Do not assume that the input file names will end in .csv'; do not add or enforce an extension. 7) 'terminate gracefully if the file cannot be found or opened' and 'validate the inputs to the main() function'; on error return empty lists / zero / empty dicts / None. 8) 2022 P2 and 2023 P2: column order may differ and extra columns may exist, so 'check for the column heading'; rows may be in random order; 'All string data in the file is case-insensitive'; 'If there is any invalid data then entire row(s) should be ignored' (negative/zero population or area, duplicate countries, empty/null names). 9) Submit a single .py named by student ID; one attempt; Moodle 'check' runs sample tests only; hidden tests after deadline; late penalty 5%/day, none after 7 days.
findings.source: brayden-blackham/Cits1401 project/README.md (P1 2020 S1); gauravcx3/Python-Numerical-Digit-Distribution-Calculator README (P2 2020 S1); Newguinea/cits1401 CITS1401 Project 1 S1 2022.pdf and Project 2 S2 2022.pdf; yogigodaraa/regional-population-statistics CITS1401 Project 2 Sem-1 2023.pdf; https://gradespire.com/cits1401-assignment-help/ (2024 P1); workingment.com snippet (2026 P1 signature def main(csvfile_1, csvfile_2, age, sa2_1, sa2_2))

findings.topic: What the no-imports rule forces students to hand-write
findings.detail: Across specs the required outputs are: per-column min/max/mean/standard deviation (formula supplied), Spearman rank correlation with alphabetical tie-breaks (2020 P1), Benford digit distributions with optional normalisation and a default parameter regularise=False (2020 P2), cosine similarity and std dev (2022 P1), 3D distances/asymmetry (2022 P2), standard error and cosine similarity per region plus nested dict {region: {country: [population, net change, % of region, density, rank]}} with rank ties broken by density then name (2023 P2), t-test scores and Minkowski distances plus nested dict by category (2024 P1), hospital data analysis (2024 S2 P2). With no csv/math/statistics module, students must: open() and readline()/for-line iterate, strip() and split(','), find header indexes, convert with int()/float() inside try/except, accumulate with loops, compute sqrt via ** 0.5, sort with list.sort(key=..., reverse=...) or hand-written sorts, and build dicts/nested dicts. The 2023 student solution confirms this pattern (readfile -> list of row dicts, stderror via ** 0.5, ZeroDivisionError handling).

findings.topic: Project marking rubric and where marks are lost
findings.detail: Marked out of 30 (scaled to 15% or 20%). 22/30 automated tests 'reflecting normal use of the program, and also how the program handles various states including error states such as different number of columns and rows'; 'You need to think creatively what your program may face'; graded on data files other than the sample. 8/30: style 5 ('use of comments, sensible variable names, your name at the top of the program'; 0 gibberish, 1-2 poor/fair, 3-4 good with small lapses, 5 excellent) and efficiency 3 ('minimise the number of times your program looks at the same data items'; 1 = 'Very poor efficiency, additional loops, inappropriate use of readline()'; 3 = 'no problem on large files'). If the marker must fix a single crash-causing bug the fixed program is scored minus 4 marks; if not readily fixable it scores zero on tests. Lab 01 style rules: identifiers at least 3 characters, meaningful, lowercase with underscores (circle_area preferred over CircleArea). Implied common loss points: missing/mis-named main(), calling print()/input(), importing csv/math, rounding mid-calculation, assuming column order or .csv suffix, crashing on missing file or bad rows, extra passes over the file, poor names/comments.
findings.source: Project specs 2020 S1, 2022 S1/S2, 2023 S1 (rubric text identical across years); Lab 01 page 3

findings.topic: Final exam format and question archetypes
findings.detail: 2021 S1 (closed book, 2 hours, 8 questions, 100 marks, 'Library modules are not allowed to be imported for any of the question'; answers hand-written in booklet): Q1 stringexpand(name) insert spaces [5]; Q2 palindrome(word) case-insensitive boolean [5]; Q3 sortdict(dict) -> list of tuples sorted by value descending, hint use sort() [10]; Q4 sumdigits(n) 'Recursion must be used... Looping is not allowed' [10]; Q5 seriesexp(x, tol) Maclaurin series summed until |term| < tol, needs factorial helper and while loop [15]; Q6 multiply_lists(lst) product over arbitrarily nested lists (recursion) [20]; Q7 team_maker(pool1,pool2,pool3) all combinations via triple nested loop, joined with spaces [15]; Q8 user_account(filename) read a comma-separated text file, find column indexes of 'First name','Last name','Date of birth' from a header whose order is unknown, build login/password strings, write logins.txt, 'terminate gracefully if there are any I/O errors' [20]. Model solutions use for/while, range(len()), list.sort(key=lambda, reverse=True), recursion with base case, try/except FileNotFoundError, readline().split(','). 2022 S2 sample (delivered online on Blackboard, 2h, 8 Q, 100 marks) is the same shape: string_combine(seq) upper-case join of mixed types [5]; extract25(nlist) filtered and sorted lists [5]; sortStaff(staff) dict -> list of tuples sorted by salary desc then name asc [7]; reverse(email) recursive reversal of each side of '@' [13]; log_cosh(tol) series with tolerance, round to 6 dp only at end [15]; extract_strings(lst) recursive flatten of nested lists/tuples keeping only strings [20]; team(ABD_dict) combinations from a dict of three offices [15]; donors(filename) two-line-per-record file parsing, totals, rank, write ranked.txt with header 'Rank,Donor,Amount', graceful I/O errors [20]. 2017 (120 marks, 8 Q) additionally had 'What does the code do? / Rewrite it so it is easier to understand' [10], 'What is seen as the result of executing the following Python code' predict-output with a dict keyed by tuples and a try/except [10], merge two sorted lists with a while loop without sort() [30], marksdistribution(D) mapping marks to N/P/Cr/D/HD bands returning a dict [30], recursive pow(x,N) with more marks for recursion. Student reviews 2023-2025 confirm the current final is 'closed-book, pen and paper', 'coding on paper', weighted 55-60%.

findings.topic: Coordinator practice sheet (typical exercise difficulty ladder)
findings.detail: 'CITS1401 practice questions, Dr Ghulam Mubashar Hassan': script printing first 100 Fibonacci numbers; Fibonacci(n) returning a list; FibonacciSum(n); FibonacciFilter(n) returning (sum, list) of terms not divisible by 2 or 5; number-to-words for 0-99; add two matrices as lists of lists; multiply matrices; mergelists([1,2,3],[4,5,6]) -> [1,4,2,5,3,6]; sortoddeven(list) odds then evens; 'functions which can generate convergent mathematical series'. Shows the unit's fondness for maths-flavoured loop problems, multiple return values, list-of-lists, and series-until-tolerance.

A 2020-era Studocu item is titled 'CITS1401 Mid-Semester Sample Test Questions and Answers' and Course Hero lists a 'Multiple-choice Mid-semester Test' with solutions; search summaries describe it as multiple choice marked by filling circles. 2020 S1 slides place it in Week 8 at 15%. The current handbook calls the hurdle a 'competency test' (must reach 50% on it to pass). Its exact 2025/2026 format and weight were not retrievable (pages blocked).

StudentVIP reviews (2023-2026): 'poorly paced, you will spend the first 4 weeks reiterating the most basic'; projects 'very difficult', 'vague instructions'; final is 'closed-book, pen and paper', 'glorified memory test', '60% of the grade'; several failures among students with no prior coding; one review lists core content as 'lists, sorting, concatenation, strings, dictionaries'; advice to practise coding by hand and not rely on AI because in-class exams are where people struggle. Implication for the app: a paper-style mode (no autocomplete, no run button, hand-trace answers) is directly useful.

recommendations: Use this ordered topic list (easy -> hard), which follows the CITS1401 lecture and lab sequence rather than a generic Python tutorial order: 1 Expressions, types and variables (arithmetic, precedence, int/float/str/bool, int()/float()/str() conversions, // and %, identifier rules) — Lab 01. 2 Definite loops and range() (for i in range, accumulators, sum/product, simple Fibonacci) — L5 and 2020 Lab 1; the unit teaches for-loops BEFORE if/else. 3 Decisions: if/elif/else, comparison and boolean operators, `in`, chained comparisons, nested-if simplification, predict-output traces — L7/L8, Lab 03. 4 Functions part 1: def/return/parameters vs arguments, docstrings, local variables, built-ins abs/round/int/len, returning booleans and strings — L9, Lab 02. 5 Strings: indexing, slicing, methods (upper/lower/strip/split/join/find/replace), ord/chr, palindromes, string building, f-strings/format — L10-L11. 6 Lists and tuples: append/insert/pop, sort()/sorted() with key and reverse, tuple packing/unpacking, multiple return values, list of lists (matrices), nested loops over lists — L12, L17, Lab 04. 7 While loops and nested loops: sentinel loops, series-until-tolerance, gcd, digit manipulation, merge two sorted lists, combinations via nested loops — L16-L18. 8 Dictionaries: get/keys/items, counting/frequency, dict -> sorted list of tuples, nested dicts, grouping by key with tie-break ranking — L20-L21, Lab 05. 9 Files and CSV by hand: open/readline/for line, strip/split(','), header-index lookup, type conversion, writing files, no csv module — L13-L14. 10 Exceptions and graceful termination: try/except FileNotFoundError, ValueError, ZeroDivisionError, returning empty/None instead of printing — L19. 11 Functions part 2 and project patterns: main(csvfile) that calls helpers, default parameters (regularise=False), no globals, no print/input, round to 4 dp only at the end, validating inputs and skipping bad rows, efficiency (single pass), style — L15 plus the project specs. 12 Recursion: base case, sum of digits, reverse string, flatten nested lists/tuples, recursive power — L27-L28, mandatory exam question. Optional late-semester extras behind the core track: sets, simulation/design, simple search (linear/binary), objects/classes.
Mark topics 1-8 as 'core / mid-semester' and 9-12 as 'late semester / project + exam' in the landing page, with project-style CSV tasks unlocked after Dictionaries.

Within each topic, mirror the three real assessment styles as tabs or tags: (a) 'Lab quiz' MCQ/select-all/predict-output/fill-in-blank with 1-mark granularity and re-check; (b) 'CodeRunner' write-a-function with a visible Test -> Result table and a penalty per failed check (0, 10, 20%); (c) 'Exam' write-a-function on a plain textarea with no run button, syntax highlighting off or minimal, a timer, and a marks weight (5/10/15/20) matching the paper, then reveal a model solution.

Embed the project rule set as a lint in the code workspace: warn on `import`, `print(` (unless inside an except branch), `input(`, `global`, hard-coded '.csv' checks, and round() inside loops; explain the marking consequence for each (zero tests, -4 marker fix, style/efficiency deductions).

Include a 'Project simulator' topic with a small synthetic CSV (header order shuffled, an extra column, a bad row, mixed case) and tasks requiring main(csvfile) to return lists/dicts rounded to 4 dp: min/max/mean/std, standard error, cosine similarity, Spearman rank with alphabetical tie-break, nested dict by region with rank ties broken by density then name. Provide reference implementations without imports.
Include a 'Recursion' topic before the final report even though it is late-semester: every final since 2017 has a mandatory recursion question ('Looping is not allowed').
Add a 'series with tolerance' and 'combinations via nested loops' question family to the while/nested loops topic; both appear in every recent final at 15 marks.

In the weak/strong report, aggregate by the same taxonomy the unit assesses: correctness on hidden tests, graceful error handling, rounding/return-type discipline, style (naming, comments, docstrings), efficiency (single pass, no repeated file reads), and hand-trace accuracy for the paper exam.
Give the code workspace a Thonny-like 'shell' echo of return values (>>> mn, mx = main('sample.csv')) since specs and labs show interaction through the Python shell, not print output.
Run student code client-side with Pyodide from cdnjs (no build step, matches the static single-HTML precedent); reject `import` lines before execution to model the Moodle marker.
